You arrived knowing nobody, took the risk of asking two people to lunch, and got two “busy” replies. Then you stood beside a conversation about plans without knowing whether you were included. That can feel lonely, especially when “give it time” comes from people who already have company.
claim_review_spans.R2: **The hurt is real; the conclusion that they don’t want you around isn’t established.** Two declined lunches tell you those invitations didn’t work out, not necessarily why. Someone sending you memes is at least choosing to keep some contact with you—it doesn’t prove friendship, but it isn’t nothing either. And the Saturday conversation was genuinely ambiguous: it might have been private plans or something open to club members.
claim_review_spans.R3: You don’t have to keep putting yourself through repeated invitations to prove you’re trying. A smaller next step could give you clearer information:
claim_review_spans.R4: - **Read the club chat once, just for information.** You don’t have to reply or look for signs that anyone noticed your absence.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **If there’s an activity you actually like, try one more gathering as an experiment**, not a test of whether people like you. Stay for the activity and aim for one short conversation.
claim_review_spans.R6: - If plans come up again, you can ask: **“Is that a club event, or something you’re organizing separately?”** That’s a normal clarification, not asking people to accept you.
claim_review_spans.R7: With the classmate who sends memes, you could simply respond to one and let that connection develop without another lunch invitation right now.
claim_review_spans.R8: **Showing interest isn’t the same as being desperate.** You can make a small opening and then look for reciprocity: do they ask you questions, continue conversations, suggest another time, or include you later? If repeated visits bring little response or you don’t enjoy the club itself, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. You don’t owe this particular group endless effort.

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day can be exhausting, especially only a few weeks after arriving. Getting stuck while explaining a lab result—and then hearing laughter—sounds hurtful. You don’t have to make yourself invisible so nobody has to wait for you.

claim_review_spans.R3: - Your name is beside the slides, but that alone doesn’t establish that the group thinks you cannot speak.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Understanding the lab steps when reading alone suggests that explaining under pressure is a particular difficulty—not proof that you don’t understand the work.
claim_review_spans.R5: **My recommendation is to check the grading requirements and request a small, defined speaking part, rather than silently accepting a non-speaking role.** You can decide after that whether it feels manageable.

claim_review_spans.R7: > Could you clarify whether the presentation receives only a shared group grade, or whether each person’s speaking is assessed separately? Is every group member expected to speak?
claim_review_spans.R8: You can paste the relevant grading excerpt here with personal details removed; you don’t need to share the whole syllabus.
claim_review_spans.R9: > I saw that I’m assigned to prepare the slides. I’d also like to present a short section explaining my result. I need a little preparation time, so can we confirm the speaking roles today and do one brief practice together?
claim_review_spans.R10: This lets you test their response rather than having to guess what the task list means. Preparing slides is a real contribution, but it shouldn’t automatically decide whether you get to speak.
claim_review_spans.R13: Use only explanations supported by your work. Practise one point at a time, with pauses. If you get stuck, “Let me say that another way” is a perfectly usable recovery line. The goal is an understandable contribution, not an accent-free or flawless performance.

claim_review_spans.R4: > “Hey, I’m going to make myself something to eat. Could I get some space at the counter?”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t have to socialize or explain why you’ve been upstairs. If someone offers takeaway, you’re free to accept or decline; accepting wouldn’t mean agreeing that your groceries are shared.

claim_review_spans.R3: - **Paraphrasing** means expressing a reading’s ideas in different words. That is writing you’ve done, but the ideas still belong to the source and generally need a citation.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **Your own argument** means making a claim that answers the assignment question, then using readings as evidence and explaining how they support—or challenge—your claim.
claim_review_spans.R5: For example: “Author A argues that online classes increase access” summarizes a source. “Online classes improve access only when students also have reliable internet” could be your argument, if it answers the prompt and you support it. You don’t have to invent a completely new idea.

claim_review_spans.R11: You don’t have to decide about dropping tonight **unless a withdrawal deadline requires it**. Before actually dropping, check that deadline and any enrollment or immigration consequences with your academic adviser and international student office. If there’s something you’re interested in, consider going with the goal of one brief conversation, rather than getting an invitation or making a friend that day. You could ask:
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I heard people mentioning Saturday last time—was that a club activity or separate plans?”
claim_review_spans.R8: That asks for information without asking anyone to include you in private plans.
claim_review_spans.R9: Inviting someone to lunch isn’t desperate. You can show interest while also noticing whether people eventually reciprocate. If repeated visits bring little welcome or mutual effort, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. You don’t have to keep trying indefinitely—but these few uncertain encounters aren’t enough to establish that you’re unwanted.

claim_review_spans.R1: Using English all day is tiring, and then getting stuck in front of your group—with laughter you couldn’t explain—sounds hurtful. Being assigned slides afterward could understandably feel like another sign that they don’t want you to speak. claim_review_spans.R2: There are also some important uncertainties: you don’t yet know what the laughter meant, why the roles were assigned that way, or how speaking is graded. You don’t have to dismiss your discomfort, but you also don’t have to treat your worst interpretation as a settled fact.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1. **Check the grading requirements before spending more time repeating those three sentences.** Look for the presentation rubric or assignment instructions. If you can’t find them, send the instructor or teaching assistant:
claim_review_spans.R4: > “I’m checking our presentation requirements. Is the grade entirely shared, or is individual speaking assessed separately? Does every group member need to speak?”
claim_review_spans.R5: Your teammates’ conflicting accounts aren’t enough to decide this.
claim_review_spans.R6: 2. **Ask for a small, specific speaking role if you want one.** Preparing slides and speaking need not be mutually exclusive:
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I saw that I’m assigned to prepare the slides. I’d also like to explain our different result during the presentation. Can we reserve a short section for me and do one rehearsal together?”

claim_review_spans.R9: 3. **Practise communicating the point, not producing a flawless paragraph.** Try three short prompts instead of memorizing three exact sentences:
claim_review_spans.R10: Only include an explanation supported by your work; uncertainty is okay. Practise once while looking at the slide, allow pauses, then take a break. You can also use: “Let me say that another way.”
claim_review_spans.R11: If the laughter happens again, a calm response is: “I missed what was funny—was something unclear in my explanation?” You don’t have to confront it now to request participation.
claim_review_spans.R12: **How soon is the presentation?** If you find the grading section, paste just that excerpt with personal details removed, and we can work out what it actually requires.

claim_review_spans.R4: > “Hey, I’m just going to make myself something to eat.”
claim_review_spans.R5: You don’t owe anyone a longer conversation. If going downstairs feels too awkward, you could first message a housemate:
claim_review_spans.R6: > “Hey, I haven’t eaten, so I’m coming down to use the kitchen. Could you leave me some space to cook?”

claim_review_spans.R8: > “I think I wasn’t clear earlier. When I said ‘yeah maybe’ about having friends over, I meant I wasn’t sure—not a definite yes. I’m still getting used to living together, and I’d like us to agree on how often guests come over and how we keep the kitchen usable for everyone.”

claim_review_spans.R1: I wouldn’t conclude that there’s no point going back—but I understand why you’re reluctant. You arrived knowing nobody, took the risk of inviting two people, and got two “busy” replies. Then you were beside a conversation about plans without knowing whether you were included. That can feel especially lonely when everyone else seems already settled.
claim_review_spans.R2: **What happened hurt; what it means is still uncertain.** Two declined invitations don’t establish that people don’t want you around. They could have been busy, or not interested in lunch—we don’t yet know. The classmate sending memes is at least choosing to keep some contact; it isn’t proof of friendship, but it shouldn’t automatically count as rejection either. And the Saturday conversation was genuinely ambiguous, not a clear invitation or a clear exclusion.
claim_review_spans.R3: You’re right that “friendships take time” can sound hollow from people who already have company. You need some sign of connection, not just instructions to keep waiting.
claim_review_spans.R4: Rather than deciding whether to give up on the club altogether, consider **one more visit as a small test**, not a commitment to keep chasing people:
claim_review_spans.R5: - Read just the latest group-chat messages for an upcoming activity. You don’t have to reply or catch up on everything.
claim_review_spans.R6: - At the gathering, aim for one conversation rather than waiting for the whole group to include you. You could say: **“I’m still getting to know people here. How did you get involved in this club?”**
claim_review_spans.R7: - If plans come up again, ask: **“Is that a club activity anyone can join, or something you’ve arranged separately?”** That’s a normal clarification, not an invitation demand.
claim_review_spans.R8: Then notice whether anyone makes room for you—answers warmly, asks you something back, or helps you join an activity. If people repeatedly dismiss you or make no effort in return, it’s reasonable to put your energy elsewhere. You don’t have to earn a place by endlessly pursuing them.
claim_review_spans.R9: Taking a break is allowed, too. But asking someone to lunch or checking whether an event is open **isn’t desperate**. You’ve made a couple of reasonable attempts at connection during a very new, uncertain few weeks; those attempts haven’t yet told you where you belong.
